title: The Story of Tavern on the Green
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro voice) trace the history of Tavern on the Green in Central Park, from its origin as a sheep fold in the 1870s, through its conversion to a restaurant by Robert Moses in 1934, its 1950s heyday, Warner LeRoy's flashy 1970s-2000s era with the Crystal Room, its closure from 2010 to 2014, and its 2014 reopening under Jim Cayola and David Salama, plus restaurant reviews and a closing co-ED sponsor read.
topics: Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux

entities.name: New York Hotel and Motel Trades Council

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts chat about New York, Studio 54, and the Saturday Night Live movie before introducing Tavern on the Green as the topic.

segments.title: Sheep fold origins and Central Park design
segments.summary: Tavern on the Green began as a sheep enclosure, the Sheep Fold, in Central Park. Its design followed the Greensward plan by Olmsted and Vaux, and the planned parade ground was replaced with the Sheep Meadow. Boss Tweed-era upgrades added a Jacob Wrey Mould-designed sheep fold, which hosted wool shearing and sheep displays.

segments.title: Sheep move to Prospect Park and 1934 restaurant announcement
segments.summary: The sheep moved to Prospect Park in 1934, reportedly over poaching fears tied to Hooverville. Robert Moses announced the conversion to a restaurant, with WPA-era CWA workers building it; the New York Times announcement is mentioned and prices were to be moderate.

segments.title: Concession leasing and taverns history
segments.summary: The Parks Department leases the restaurant to outside concessionaires through public bidding with licensing fees. The CWA paved the former sheep area with flagstones as an outdoor summer dining space. The name nods to New York's eighteenth-century taverns and pleasure gardens.

segments.title: World War II police headquarters and 1940s-1950s growth
segments.summary: During World War II the building served as headquarters for the City Patrol Corps made of volunteers. Year-round operation began in 1943, and the restaurant expanded in the 1950s to about 21,000 square feet with the Elm Tree Room, seating up to 1,200 guests. A 1950 live album, Dancing at the Tavern on the Green, was recorded and white lights were first wrapped around trees.
topics: Dancing at the Tavern on the Green album

segments.title: 1956 playground fight and Joe Baum era
segments.summary: In 1956 Robert Moses sought a parking lot on a half acre parkland, prompting mothers to protest and win an injunction; Moses set aside fifty thousand dollars for a playground, the West 67th Street Playground. Joe Baum took over the lease in the 1960s and ran several famous restaurants.

segments.title: Warner LeRoy takes over and Maxwell's Plum
segments.summary: Central Park's reputation declined in the 1970s. Warner LeRoy took over the lease in 1974, bringing the flashy style of Maxwell's Plum, a theatrical, eclectic, no-dress-code restaurant. He spent about ten million dollars renovating.

segments.title: 1976 opening day and the Crystal Room
segments.summary: Opening-day excess included a giant Sunday, a champagne bottle flown in with its own seat on Air France, and a sixteen-foot Central Park cake. LeRoy brought in French chefs and Indian chandeliers and built the glass Crystal Room, featured in films such as Ghostbusters, Arthur and Beaches. Critic Pete Wells later called it a wedding cake palace.

segments.title: Crystal Room heyday, illegal expansion and sponsor break
segments.summary: Under LeRoy the restaurant was highly profitable, with forty million dollars in revenue annually in the 1990s and about 600,000 diners a year. The city allowed the Crystal Room expansion without a building permit, with a one point two million dollar license fee. A break followed.

segments.title: Labor issues and decline after 2000
segments.summary: LeRoy's staff was not unionized until a 1989 walkout. Warner LeRoy died in February 2001, and then September 11 hit New York. Jennifer LeRoy ran the restaurant, but food reviews were poor and it declined by the mid-2000s.
topics: decline of Tavern on the Green

segments.title: Reviews, lawsuit and lease non-renewal
segments.summary: The New York Times reviewed the restaurant five times, never above one star out of four. A 2008 lawsuit alleged sexual and racial harassment, and in 2010 the Parks Department did not renew the Leroy family's license.

segments.title: Closure 2010 to 2014 and gift shop
segments.summary: The restaurant sat vacant from 2010 to 2014. Dean Poll backed out of negotiations with the union, bidders were scared off, and Mayor Bloomberg turned the space into a gift shop and information center.

segments.title: 2014 reopening by Cayola and Salama
segments.summary: In 2012 the city chose Jim Cayola and David Salama of Philadelphia, who invested ten million dollars to strip the Leroy decor and restore a nineteenth-century tavern look. Critics questioned the deal, and the hosts noted family and political connections involving Bloomberg's deputy mayor.

segments.title: Auction and 2014 reviews
segments.summary: Leroy decor was auctioned in the Crystal Room. After the 2014 opening, New York outlets panned the food, though critics were understanding about serving large crowds. Executive chef Katie Sparks is mentioned.

segments.title: Chuck's personal review and menu
segments.summary: Chuck describes his recent visit: the menu included crab cake, calamari, Dorset sheep steak, scallops, salmon, and lemon thyme chicken. He found the food fine, the service good, the martini good, and called the place touristy but worth a visit once.

segments.title: Co-ED sponsor appeal and sign-off
segments.summary: In lieu of listener mail, the hosts promote the co-ED Cooperative, which sponsors students in rural Guatemala for twenty dollars a month, and a giving-day Zoom hangout. They also give listener email contact details.
